title: What I Learned from Studying Abroad at Tulane University
paragraphs: The reason I studied abroad was that I wanted to experience American medical education, said to be of a high level, and to be stimulated while still a student. I had a vague expectation that by experiencing a world I did not know and coming into contact with styles and values different from Japan's, I would deepen my understanding of the world, rethink what is common sense in Japan, become interested in something new that I had not expected, study as my interest led me, and increase my future possibilities. In that context, I was allowed to study abroad at Tulane University in New Orleans, in the United States. At Tulane University, I did clerkships of one month each in cardiology, nephrology and pulmonary medicine.

In cardiology, one inpatient was assigned to me the day before, and the daily routine was to go and meet the patient early in the morning, take the history and physical findings, write a draft treatment plan in the chart, present it to the resident, then follow the attending rounds and present again, and in the afternoon take lectures on reading EKGs and echocardiograms with the many other exchange students and local students, or take part in conferences. The discussions, including the presentations, always required answers and their objective grounds, and students too were required to know their own patients' information in detail. Not to mention the local students, the exchange students were also far superior in medical knowledge, ability to gather information and ability to discuss in English, and carried out the daily routine as a matter of course, which overwhelmed me, but a kind younger Indian exchange student helped me at first, almost as an interpreter, and somehow I managed to get through the work after a fashion. He and I studied together in my room every day, talked about our future dreams as physicians and about each other's cultures and histories, and became good friends.

In nephrology, one or two patients were assigned to me, and after taking the history and physical examination early in the morning and writing the chart, I was allowed to present directly every day to the attending, who was the person in charge, at the attending rounds. My assessment and treatment were often adopted as they were, and although looking things up was hard, it gave me great confidence. In the afternoon I observed the clinic and took part in the renal biopsy pathology conference and study sessions for specialists. There open discussion took place regardless of age or status, and it was very impressive to see even residents and students speak their opinions to senior physicians and actively take part in the discussion.

In pulmonary medicine, I followed the supervising doctor, wrote charts and observed procedures such as bronchoscopy and thoracentesis. In free time, the doctors enthusiastically gave lectures on topics such as the use of antibiotics in infectious diseases and pulmonary function tests, and I was also given the opportunity to present a paper. I was also able to see diseases rarely seen in Japan, such as cystic fibrosis.

Overall, there are three things I learned from studying abroad. The first was that I was able to see the practice of education that is not one-way but two-way. When learning something, it is not always the senior teaching the junior; rather, each has their own view based on objective evidence that they have reached themselves, and the truth of it is decided through discussion. I learned this way of learning, which requires an ability to discuss that a mere listing of knowledge cannot match, and it seemed very rational.

The second was that I noticed the common direction in which American and Japanese medicine are heading. I saw many differences in insurance and other systems, but I felt commonalities on the contrary. Doctors provide the maximum treatment possible at the time from the resources they can have, and, aiming to improve treatment outcomes for the next generation, quietly advance basic and clinical research in order to move medicine forward. This attitude was seen in common amid the many differences.

The third was that I was able to come into contact with the values and cultures of people from various countries. As the United States is said to be a melting pot of races, there are many second- and third-generation people and exchange students, and I was able to communicate with them in English and come into contact with many values and ways of thinking that I could never have known before. As a result, I now have colleagues studying the same discipline of medicine in various parts of the world, and I could feel a bond beyond countries, that we will work from now on facing the same direction toward the same goal, which I believe will be a great asset supporting me in the future.
I would like to make use of the many experiences and the motivation I gained through study abroad in various situations in the future. Thank you very much to everyone who supported my study abroad.
